appraisal_events.evidence: « D'ailleurs Mme de Guermantes faisait seulement en ceci de l'esprit, et du plus faux, car la reine de Naples, comme la duchesse d'Alençon, morte tragiquement aussi, avait un grand cœur et a sincèrement pleuré les siens. Mme de Guermantes connaissait trop les nobles sœurs bavaroises, ses cousines, pour l'ignorer. »
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator breaks in to disqualify the duchesse's salon anecdote (« Je voudrais qu'elle perdît une sœur tous les jours ! ») as wit of the falsest kind, and adds that she knew the truth perfectly well — so the mockery rebounds on her as knowing slander while the reine de Naples is vindicated.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Vous savez bien que vous ne le verrez pas, Oriane […] Robert pourrait ce qu'il voudrait sur Monserfeuil. Seulement, comme il ne sait pas ce qu'il veut, il le fait demander par nous, parce qu'il sait qu'il n'y a pas de meilleure manière de faire échouer la chose. »
appraisal_events.explanation: Cutting across his wife's evasive « Mon Dieu, si je le vois », the duc publicly blames Robert as irresolute and self-defeating and thereby kills the Morocco request the princesse de Parme was pressing on his behalf; the narrator frames the outburst as a calculated manoeuvre (« pour forcer la princesse à retirer sa demande »), which ironizes the stated grounds without softening the refusal.

status_effects.explanation: The narrator's direct correction turns her prized esprit into demonstrable falseness and heartlessness about a real bereavement, an unusually explicit authorial mark against her.

Her double performance collapses within the same scene: the wit is voided by the narrator, and her evasive amiability about Monserfeuil (« Très peu », though she is « intimement liée » with him) is overridden aloud by her husband, who interrupts her and contradicts her before the princesse.
Against the salon mockery, the narrator credits her with « un grand cœur » and sincere grief, so the passage ends by defending rather than exposing her.
In absentia he is characterized by his uncle as not knowing what he wants and as arranging his own failure, and his petition dies in the room without anyone speaking for him.

Her intercession, seized on as soon as Mme de Guermantes involuntarily hands her the name Robert « comme une perche », is talked down by the duc into withdrawal; she gets no commitment and is managed rather than answered.

ambiguities: The duc's tirade is explicitly staged by the narrator as tactical — designed to make Mme de Parme drop the request while leaving the duchesse's amiability unimpeached and loading the refusal onto his own « caractère essentiellement quinteux ». It is therefore undecidable whether his contempt for Robert's irresolution is sincere judgment or pretext; the blame is scored as landing on Robert either way, since the refusal it produces is real.

Whether the duc's interruption lowers the duchesse or protects her is genuinely double-edged: he contradicts her in front of a princess, yet the stated purpose of the manoeuvre is to preserve her reputation for amiability. The modest rhetorical_position penalty reflects the public override; a reading that weighted the protective intent would leave her rhetorical standing flat.
